metaTitle: Types of Pallets: Stringer vs. Block, Entry Types, Decks, and Materials — AGL Pallet
metaDescription: The main types of pallets explained: stringer and block construction, two-way and four-way entry, deck styles, wood, plastic, presswood, metal, and corrugated pallets, and how to choose.

sections.heading: Stringer vs. block construction
paragraphs: Almost every wood pallet is one of two constructions. The difference is what holds the decks apart.

table.caption: Stringer and block pallets compared
rows: Continuous boards (stringers) running the length, usually three on a 48 × 40
Blocks, usually nine on a 48 × 40, tied together by stringerboards
Two-way, or partial four-way when the stringers are notched
True four-way for forklifts and pallet jacks
Fewer parts; simpler to build and repair
More parts; more labor per pallet
One-way and domestic shipping; the GMA 48 × 40
Pooled programs, automated handling, many export lanes
table.note: Typical characteristics. A heavy stringer design can outperform a light block design; the spec decides, not the category.

after: See [GMA pallets and grades](/resources/gma-pallets-and-grades/) for the 48 × 40 stringer footprint, and [pooled vs. owned pallets](/resources/pooled-vs-owned-pallets/) for the block pallets used in rental pools.

sections.heading: Two-way, partial four-way, and true four-way

table.caption: Pallet entry types
rows: Notches cut in the bottom of the stringers
Blocks with open space between them, and a bottom deck that leaves wheel openings
table.note: Notches let forklift tines in from the side, but pallet jack wheels need an opening in the bottom deck, which a notched stringer pallet does not have on its long sides.

after: Entry matters most at the receiving dock. A distribution center that turns pallets with pallet jacks, or runs automated equipment, may require true four-way entry.

sections.heading: Deck styles
list: Single-face: a top deck only. A skid is the simplest case. See [skid vs. pallet](/resources/skid-vs-pallet/).
Double-face, nonreversible: top and bottom decks, with the bottom deck lighter or more open than the top. The most common style for stringer pallets.
Double-face, reversible: identical top and bottom decks, so either side can carry the load.
Flush: deckboards end even with the outer stringers or blocks.
Single-wing or double-wing: deckboards extend past the outer stringers on the top deck, or on both decks, for sling or crane handling.
Solid or closed deck: boards laid with no gaps, or a sheet deck, for small cartons, bags, or loads that must not snag.
after: Deck coverage and board thickness drive both strength and weight. See the [pallet weight estimator](/resources/pallet-calculators/pallet-weight-estimator/) to see how board count changes an estimate.

sections.heading: Pallet materials
paragraphs: Wood carries most North American freight. Other materials fit specific jobs.

table.caption: Pallet materials at a glance
rows: General freight, custom sizes, heavy loads, one-way and multi-trip
Weight and moisture vary; can splinter or mold if stored wet
Closed loops, food and pharma, automated systems
Higher upfront cost; custom sizes tied to molds; hard to repair
Light one-way export loads; often nestable
Very heavy loads, high heat, sanitary or closed-loop uses
Light one-way loads, air freight, displays
table.note: Export status is summarized from the ISPM 15 scope. Destination countries can add rules; confirm before shipping. See [heat-treated pallets and ISPM-15](/resources/heat-treated-pallets-ispm-15/).

sections.heading: Special-purpose pallets
list: Drum pallets: square footprints such as 48 × 48 or 42 × 42 sized to hold drums. See [pallet sizes](/resources/pallet-sizes/).
Half and quarter pallets: small footprints for store displays and light loads.
Export pallets: heat treated and stamped for ISPM 15, sometimes block construction to suit the destination's handling.
Engineered and heavy-duty pallets: designed to a specific load, rack span, or handling system. See [custom and engineered pallets](/custom-engineered/).
Crates and skids: for machinery and loads that need protection on all sides or ship on runners.

sections.heading: Choosing a pallet type
paragraphs: Start from the load and both ends of the trip, not from the pallet:
list: What does the unit load weigh, and is the weight even or concentrated?
How is it handled at the shipping and receiving docks: forklift, pallet jack, conveyor, or automated equipment?
Will it be stacked or racked, and on what span?
Does the pallet come back, or ship once?
Does the receiver require a specific footprint, entry type, or pool?
after: AGL sources new wood pallets: stock and custom stringer and block pallets, engineered skids, and crates, placed with qualified mills. See [products](/products/).

items.question: What is the difference between a stringer pallet and a block pallet?
answer: A stringer pallet rests on continuous boards that run its length, so it allows two-way entry, or partial four-way if the stringers are notched. A block pallet rests on blocks, so forklifts and pallet jacks can enter from all four sides. Block pallets cost more and are common in pools and automated handling.

items.question: What is a four-way pallet?
answer: A pallet that forklifts can enter from all four sides. On a notched stringer pallet (partial four-way), pallet jacks still enter only the two ends. On a block pallet (true four-way), both forklifts and pallet jacks enter from every side.

items.question: What is the most common type of pallet?
answer: In North America, the 48 × 40 wood stringer pallet, the GMA footprint, is the most common by a wide margin. Block pallets of the same footprint dominate rental pools.
